title: The trend of SMOKE-PM2.5 and its association with drought
text:
Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) from wildfire smoke is an important contributor to air pollution in the United States, particularly in the West, with important implications for public health and air quality management. Human-caused ignitions have extended the U.S. wildfire season beyond the period traditionally associated with lightning-caused fires (Balch et al., 2017). As wildfire activity and smoke emissions may change over time, understanding long-term trends in smoke-related PM₂.₅ is important for identifying changes in population exposure and informing air quality management.
Drought is a potential influence on the seasonal patterns of wildfire smoke. By reducing vegetation and fuel moisture, drought can create conditions favorable for wildfire activity and associated smoke emissions. Wang et al. (2022) found that increasing summer PM₂.₅ concentrations in the northwestern United States were primarily driven by increases in total carbonaceous aerosols, with stronger trends under drought conditions. This suggests that drought may play an important role in shaping long-term changes in smoke-related PM₂.₅.
This study will examine long-term trends in wildfire smoke PM₂.₅ across California during summer and fall, the primary seasons of wildfire activity. Sen’s slope and the Mann-Kendall test will be used to characterize spatial trends from 2006 to 2023. Pixel-level Pearson correlation analysis will then examine the associations between drought conditions and smoke-related PM₂.₅, identifying their spatial patterns across California.

title: The trend of SMOKE-PM2.5 and its association with drought
text:
2.1 Materials

Daily 10km wildfire smoke PM2.5 data, 2006-2023
This machine-learning product has an overall R² of 0.63, with performance varying regionally (Childs et al., 2022). A zero prediction indicates a smoke day without elevated PM₂.₅. Data are available from the Environmental change and Human Outcomes lab.
Drought data
Monthly Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) data at 4 km resolution combine precipitation and potential evapotranspiration to characterize drought (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010). More negative values indicate greater drought severity, while positive values indicate wetter conditions (Table 1). The SPEI data can be access through National Integrated Drought Information

Calculate seasonal mean daily smoke PM2.5, retain only summer and fall observations, and return a dataframe containing the Year, Season, and Grid_ID combinations.


Show Code
grid_ids <- unique(dailysmoke$grid_id_10km)
smoke_season <- dailysmoke |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), Year = year(date), month = month(date)) |>
  filter(month %in% 6:11) |>
  mutate(Season = if_else(month <= 8, "summer", "fall")) |>
  group_by(grid_id_10km, Year, Season) |>
  # Sum recorded predictions; omitted zero-smoke days add nothing to the sum.
  summarise(aggsmokePM_pred = sum(smokePM_pred, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Divide by all calendar days: summer = 92, fall = 91.
  mutate(dailysmokePM_pred = aggsmokePM_pred/if_else(Season == "summer", 92, 91)) |>
  # Fill entirely absent grid-year-season combinations with zero.
  complete(grid_id_10km = grid_ids, Year = 2006:2023, Season = c("summer", "fall"), 
           fill = list(dailysmokePM_pred = 0))

Convert the seasonal mean smoke data into raster format.


Show Code
library(sf)
library(terra)

# 1. Inspect the sf object
# cat("## 1. Inspect the spatial data\n\n")
# cat("- Geometry type:", paste(unique(st_geometry_type(smokeCA)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
# cat("- CRS:", st_crs(smokeCA)$input, "\n")
# cat("- Number of features:", nrow(smokeCA), "\n")
# cat("- Number of attributes:", ncol(st_drop_geometry(smokeCA)), "\n\n")

# Check attribute columns
# print(names(smokeCA))

# Transform the 10-km grid to EPSG:5070
smokeCA_proj <- st_transform(smokeCA, 5070)

# Convert sf to SpatVector
smokeCA_vect <- terra::vect(smokeCA_proj)

# Align the extent to a fixed 10-km grid so cells are exactly square.
cell_size <- 10000
grid_extent <- as.vector(terra::ext(smokeCA_vect))
x_min <- floor(grid_extent[1] / cell_size) * cell_size
x_max <- ceiling(grid_extent[2] / cell_size) * cell_size
y_min <- floor(grid_extent[3] / cell_size) * cell_size
y_max <- ceiling(grid_extent[4] / cell_size) * cell_size
r <- terra::rast(
  nrows = as.integer(round((y_max - y_min) / cell_size)),
  ncols = as.integer(round((x_max - x_min) / cell_size)),
  xmin = x_min, xmax = x_max,
  ymin = y_min, ymax = y_max,
  crs = terra::crs(smokeCA_vect))
stopifnot(all(abs(terra::res(r) - cell_size) < 1e-8))


# Get unique seasons and years
# Use consecutive years from the earliest to the latest observed year.
years <- seq.int(min(smokeCA_proj$Year, na.rm = TRUE), max(smokeCA_proj$Year, na.rm = TRUE))
seasons <- sort(unique(na.omit(as.character(smokeCA_proj$Season))))
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

for (ss in seasons) {
  # Initialize one NA band per year so missing combinations retain their positions.
  pm25_season <- terra::rast(r, nlyrs = length(years), vals = NA_real_)

  for (i in seq_along(years)) {
    sub_grid <- smokeCA_proj |> filter(Year == years[i], Season == ss)
    if (nrow(sub_grid) == 0) next

    # Write the existing seasonal means into the corresponding annual band.
    pm25_season[[i]] <- terra::rasterize(terra::vect(sub_grid), r, field = "dailysmokePM_pred")}

  names(pm25_season) <- paste0("dailysmokePM_pred", years)
  output_file <- file.path(
    "data",
    paste0("PM25_CA_", ss, ".tif"))

  # Write raster
  terra::writeRaster(
    pm25_season,
    output_file,
    overwrite = TRUE)}

title: The trend of SMOKE-PM2.5 and its association with drought
section: 3.1 Annual Spatial Mean of Smoke PM2.5
text:
3.1 Annual Spatial Mean of Smoke PM2.5
Mean daily wildfire smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations showed distinct seasonal spatial patterns (Figure 2). In summer, higher concentrations were more widespread across northern California. In fall, elevated concentrations were more localized, with prominent hotspots in northern and central-eastern California. Coastal areas and much of southern California generally had lower concentrations in both seasons.








Figure 2: California-wide spatial mean of seasonal daily wildfire smoke \(\mathrm{PM}_{2.5}\) concentrations for summer and fall, 2006–2023.

title: The trend of SMOKE-PM2.5 and its association with drought
section: 3.2 Overall Annual Temporary Trends in Smoke PM2.5
text:
3.2 Overall Annual Temporary Trends in Smoke PM2.5
As shown in Figure 3, California-wide seasonal mean daily wildfire smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations were generally low before 2016, except for a summer peak in 2008 that coincided with widespread lightning-triggered fires.
Variability increased during 2017-2021, with the highest fall concentration in 2020 (15.70 µg/m³) and the highest summer concentration in 2021 (10.64 µg/m³). These peaks coincided with major wildfire activity, including the August Complex and Creek fires in 2020 and the Dixie and Caldor fires in 2021. Drought, extreme heat, and reduced snowpack likely helped create conditions favorable for severe wildfire activity in 2021. The Concentrations declined sharply in 2022-2023, highlighting the influence of episodic high-smoke years.








Figure 3: spatial mean of seasonal daily smoke pm2.5 concentrations for summer and fall

title: The trend of SMOKE-PM2.5 and its association with drought
text:
3.3 Spatial Trends in Smoke PM2.5


Show Code
library(terra)
library(trend)
library(Kendall)

calc_sen <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (length(x) < 10) return(NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(x)) == 1) return(0)
  unname(trend::sens.slope(x)$estimates)}

calc_mk <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  if (length(x) < 10) return(NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(x)) == 1) return(NA_real_)
  unname(Kendall::MannKendall(x)$sl)}

# Calculate Sen's slope
summer_sen <- app(summer, fun = calc_sen)
fall_sen   <- app(fall, fun = calc_sen)
# Calculate Mann-Kendall p-values
summer_mk <- app(summer, fun = calc_mk)
fall_mk   <- app(fall, fun = calc_mk)

# Combine slope and p-value into two bands.
summer_result <- c(summer_sen, summer_mk)
fall_result <- c(fall_sen, fall_mk)
names(summer_result) <- c("Sen_slope", "MK_pvalue")
names(fall_result) <- c("Sen_slope", "MK_pvalue")

# Save one two-band GeoTIFF per season.
# writeRaster(summer_result, "data/PM25_CA_summer_trend.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
# writeRaster(fall_result, "data/PM25_CA_fall_trend.tif", overwrite = TRUE)


As shown in Figure 4, smoke PM₂.₅ concentrations generally increased across most of California. The largest summer increases occurred in northwestern California, while fall increases were most pronounced in northern and east-central California. Statistically significant increases were observed in both seasons.


Show Code
# Plot the summer and fall trend
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)


# Calculate a shared, symmetric color scale for both trend maps.
slope_range <- terra::global(
  c(summer_result[[1]], fall_result[[1]]),
  "range",
  na.rm = TRUE)

slope_limit <- max(abs(as.matrix(slope_range)), na.rm = TRUE)
if (!is.finite(slope_limit) || slope_limit == 0) slope_limit <- 1

# Common map theme.
map_theme <- theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.margin = margin(6, 10, 6, 10),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9))

# Plot Sen's slope.
plot_slope <- function(x, title) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = x) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#2166AC", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#B2182B",
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-slope_limit, slope_limit),
      name = expression(atop("Sen's slope", "(" * mu * "g/" * m^3 * ")/year")),
      na.value = "transparent") +
    labs(title = title) +
    map_theme}

# Plot Mann-Kendall significance.
plot_significance <- function(x, title) {
  sig <- terra::ifel(x < 0.05, 1, 0)
  sig <- as.factor(sig)
  levels(sig) <- data.frame(
    ID = c(0, 1),
    Significance = c("Not significant", "Significant"))
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = sig, show.legend = TRUE) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(
        "Not significant" = "grey80",
        "Significant" = "#D55E00"
      ),
      breaks = c("Not significant", "Significant"),
      drop = FALSE,
      na.translate = FALSE,
      name = "MK significance",
      na.value = "transparent"
    ) +
    labs(title = title) +
    map_theme}

# Arrange the four maps.
plots <- list(
  plot_slope(summer_result[[1]], "Summer trend"),
  plot_significance(summer_result[[2]], "Summer significance"),
  plot_slope(fall_result[[1]], "Fall trend"),
  plot_significance(fall_result[[2]], "Fall significance"))

p <- patchwork::wrap_plots(
  plots,
  ncol = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
print(p)
# ggsave("data/PM25_CA_trend_2x2.png", p, width = 10, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

section: 3.4 The Association between Drought and Smoke PM2.5
text:
3.4 The Association between Drought and Smoke PM2.5


Show Code
library(terra)
drought_index <- rast("data/nclimgrid-spei-pearson-01_CA.nc")
dates <- time(drought_index)
years <- as.integer(format(dates, "%Y"))
months <- as.integer(format(dates, "%m"))

# cat("Date range:", range(dates), "\n")
# cat("Month range:", range(months), "\n")
get_seasonal_spei <- function(season_months, season_name) {
  idx <- which(years %in% 2006:2023 & months %in% season_months)
  for (y in 2006:2023) {
    observed <- months[idx][years[idx] == y]
    if (!identical(sort(observed), as.integer(season_months))) {
      stop(sprintf("Missing or duplicate months: %s %d", season_name, y))
    }
  }
  result <- tapp(drought_index[[idx]], index = years[idx], fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  names(result) <- paste0("SPEI_", season_name, "_", 2006:2023)
  return(result)
}

# Average June–August and September–November for each year.
drought_summer <- get_seasonal_spei(6:8, "summer")
drought_fall <- get_seasonal_spei(9:11, "fall")
# print(drought_summer)
# print('--------------------')
# print(drought_fall)

# Save 18 annual bands for each season, covering 2006-2023.
writeRaster(drought_summer, "data/SPEI_CA_summer.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
writeRaster(drought_fall, "data/SPEI_CA_fall.tif", overwrite = TRUE)




Show Code
library(terra)
# The season mean drought index above has a spatial resolution of 4km, whereas our # PM2.5 data has a spatial resolution of 10km. Now, re sample the drought index to # the resolution of pm2.5.

# Read seasonal rasters.
summer <- rast("data/PM25_CA_summer.tif")
fall <- rast("data/PM25_CA_fall.tif")
drought_summer <- rast("data/SPEI_CA_summer.tif")
drought_fall <- rast("data/SPEI_CA_fall.tif")

# Match the CRS, resolution, extent and alignment of each PM2.5 grid.
align_drought <- function(drought, pm25) {
  target <- pm25[[1]]
  if (crs(drought) == "" || crs(target) == "") {
    stop("Missing CRS information.")
  }
  cat("Same CRS:", same.crs(drought, target), "\n")
  if (same.crs(drought, target)) {
    result <- resample(drought, target, method = "average")
  } else {
    result <- project(drought, target, method = "average")
  }
  names(result) <- names(drought)
  stopifnot(compareGeom(result[[1]], target, res = TRUE))
  return(result)
}

drought_summer_10km <- align_drought(drought_summer, summer)

Both seasons showed substantial interannual variability for drought index (Figure 5). Notably, SPEI reached its lowest values in 2020 and 2021, indicating more severe drought conditions during these two years.


Show Code
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

get_annual_mean <- function(r, season) {
  layer_years <- as.integer(stringr::str_extract(names(r), "[0-9]{4}$"))
  if (anyNA(layer_years) || anyDuplicated(layer_years)) {
    stop("Each raster band must end with a unique four-digit year.")
  }
  x <- terra::global(r, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(Year = layer_years, Mean_SPEI = x$mean, Season = season)
}

annual_spei <- bind_rows(
  get_annual_mean(drought_summer_10km, "Summer"),
  get_annual_mean(drought_fall_10km, "Fall")
) |>
  mutate(Season = factor(Season, levels = c("Summer", "Fall"))) |>
  arrange(Season, Year)

p_annual <- ggplot(
  annual_spei,
  aes(x = Year, y = Mean_SPEI, color = Season, linetype = Season, shape = Season)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Summer" = "#D55E00", "Fall" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(c(
    seq(min(annual_spei$Year), max(annual_spei$Year), by = 2),
    max(annual_spei$Year)
  )))) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Variation in Seasonal SPEI",
    x = "Year",
    y = "California-wide mean SPEI"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

print(p_annual)








Figure 5: Mean drought index from 2006 to 2023 for summer and fall in California







Show Code
# Calculate the pixel-level personal coefficient between season pm2.5 and drought.
# Match bands to 2006-2023 using the year at the end of each band name.
match_years <- function(r) {
  years <- as.integer(sub(".*([0-9]{4})$", "\\1", names(r)))
  if (anyNA(years) || anyDuplicated(years) || !all(2006:2023 %in% years)) {
    stop("Check band names: each band must end with a unique year covering 2006–2023.")
  }
  return(r[[match(2006:2023, years)]])
}

# Calculate the temporal Pearson correlation at each pixel.
pixel_pearson <- function(pm25, drought) {
  pm25 <- match_years(pm25)
  drought <- match_years(drought)
  stopifnot(compareGeom(pm25, drought, lyrs = TRUE, crs = TRUE, res = TRUE))
  n <- nlyr(pm25)

  result <- app(c(pm25, drought), fun = function(v) {
    x <- v[seq_len(n)]
    y <- v[n + seq_len(n)]
    valid <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
    x <- x[valid]
    y <- y[valid]
    # Return NA for fewer than 3 paired years or constant values.
    if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0 || sd(y) == 0) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
    return(cor(x, y, method = "pearson"))
  })
  names(result) <- "Pearson_r"
  return(result)
}

cor_summer <- pixel_pearson(summer, drought_summer_10km)
cor_fall <- pixel_pearson(fall, drought_fall_10km)


Figure 6 shows the Pearson correlation between PM2.5 and drought index for summer and fall. Smoke PM₂.₅ and SPEI were negatively correlated across most of California in both summer and fall, indicating that drier years generally had higher smoke concentrations. Correlations were stronger and more widespread in fall, while summer showed greater spatial variation, with weaker correlations along parts of the coast and in southern California.








Figure 6: Pixel-wise Pearson correlation between PM₂.₅ and drought index during summer and #fall, 2006-2023.
